item.title: From Competition to Inspiration: Turning Envy Into Growth
item.description:
Jealousy

From Competition to Inspiration: Turning Envy Into Growth

Discover how to transform competitive envy into motivation and inspiration.

Posted June 19, 2026

Key points
  • Pay attention to physical and emotional signs of competitive envy.
  • Identify where feelings of inadequacy or comparison began.
  • Challenge assumptions and separate fact from speculation.
  • Use competitive envy as a tool for growth rather than rivalry.
Competitive envy can get in the way of enjoying our lives.
Source: Ben Iwara / Unsplash

Recently, I received an email from someone who read my article The Psychology of Competitiveness and asked, “what practical steps can someone take to shift from feeling competitive with another person to feeling inspired by them instead?” I thought it was a great question. Who hasn’t felt envious competition at some point?

Competition is a normal human behavior. Some of us are wired to be more competitive than others — it’s baked into our personality. An issue arises when competition turns us into someone we don’t recognize, or it creates a grudge that won’t go away. It may also be that instead of encouraging you towards self-improvement, competitive envy is holding you back.

You may become competitive or envious of your coworker who just received a promotion. Or you may see someone’s social media posts and wonder why you can’t have a life like theirs. You may be praised for your artistic skills, but someone has joined your friend group who has won awards for their work.

Sometimes our brain views others as a threat when they might have something we don’t or be better at something than we are.

Notice Your Physical Reactions

What does your body feel like when you are around this person or hear about this person’s success? What feelings come up for you? Is it causing you health issues, like headaches and stomachaches? Ask yourself when these feelings show up. Is it when you are looking at their social media? Is it when you hear a friend telling you about how great this person is? What are the triggers? Try relaxation exercises, such as deep breathing or a walk, to reduce the intensity of your emotions. Being active can also help you process how you are feeling.

Find the Origin

When we have competitive feelings that turn into envy, it says more about us than about them. Are you feeling inferior or like you can’t do anything right? When did you first feel this way? When you were a child, did you have caregivers or other adults in your life who told you that you weren’t good enough? Were you treated as “less than” compared to other family members? Usually, feelings of envy run deep, and you may consider speaking to a mental health professional (MHP). An MHP can help you process feelings that go back to your family of origin and help you make better sense of how you are feeling in the present.

article continues after advertisement

Separate Fact from Speculation

Part of competition and envy is thinking that the other person is having an amazing life. Why can’t we have things that good? The truth is that we never really know what goes on behind closed doors. As the saying goes, every person is fighting a war we know nothing about. When the narrative “Why do they have such a perfect life?” pops up, ask yourself: Is this a fact or a speculation? Just because someone posts on social media doesn’t mean that it’s real. You may be surprised by how much your brain relies on speculation rather than facts.

What Is Your End Goal?

Is this someone with whom you see yourself having a long-term friendship or relationship? If so, it may be beneficial to take a step back and see if competition is getting in the way of you getting to know them better. If your end goal is to be “better” at something than this person, ask yourself what will happen if you do become better. Will it make you happy? Give your life meaning? Or will it be a temporary feeling of winning, followed by more competition?

What Other Factors Are at Play?

You may be competitive with someone who has narcissistic tendencies. They may have set up a competition by comparing you with others, and you always seem to fall short. You may be striving to be the person they say that you are not. It might be that the best course of action for you is to limit your contact with this person. If your interactions with this person leave you feeling confused, anxious, or less than, it may be time to take a step back.

article continues after advertisement

What Can You Learn From This Person?

If you are feeling competitive and envious of someone who seems to have no trouble making friends, ask yourself what you might learn from them. You may be feeling competitive or envious because having more friends is something you really want in your life. What might they be doing to meet people? Maybe they belong to social groups, like a book club, or maybe they volunteer. If you get to know this person better, you might even feel comfortable asking them how they get to know others. If you are feeling competitive envy over someone’s seemingly perfect health, maybe this is an opportunity to see how you could improve your quality of life. Sometimes our competitiveness and envy can get in the way of learning more about others and ourselves.

Reach Out

If the person you are competing with isn’t a friend or family member, consider making a friendly overture. If you already have a healthy level of emotional intimacy with this person, consider being honest and saying, “I admit, I get envious of how clean your house is.” Many times, the person will respond that they actually have been envious of something in your life. Reaching out can help you recognize that others share the same feelings and experiences as you do.

item.title: How to Locate Your Own Hero’s Journey Narrative
item.description:
Resilience

How to Locate Your Own Hero’s Journey Narrative

It's easier to pace yourself day to day when you grasp just where you're going.

Posted June 19, 2026

Key points
  • Reflecting on your own "hero's journey" narrative boosts your resilience and sense of meaning in life.
  • Locating this narrative is a smart long-term pacing strategy because it reminds you where you're headed.
  • Regularly revisiting your narrative can restore focus and reveal new insights.

From epic poets onward, storytellers have understood their art’s clarifying function as boiling events down to their essence and underscoring what’s most vital. Narratives “connect certain elements. They go, ‘That thing I did five years ago led me to who I am today,’” says Boston College management professor Benjamin Rogers. “That’s the power of the way we tell our stories."

Tracing our own personal narratives, Rogers has found, not only adds meaning to our lives — it helps us align our day-to-day choices with clear guiding principles when life gets tough.

Source: jplenio / pixabay

Rogers has spent years studying the role life narratives play in helping people understand not just what matters to them, but how their guiding focus came to be. He's discovered that the "hero's journey" story structure is especially good at revealing the central themes that animate people’s lives.

Sometimes known as a “monomyth,” a hero’s journey story features a character who sets out on an adventure, triumphs over obstacles along the way, and comes back transformed, bringing something valuable back to the community. Classic stories from around the world, from Homer’s Odyssey to the Mesopotamian Epic of Gilgamesh, closely follow this basic template.

Rogers suspected that hero’s journey–style storytelling might be a powerful vehicle for helping people understand their experiences and clarify their ultimate goals. To test this theory, he and his colleagues enrolled hundreds of people in a re-storying exercise in which they rewrote their own life stories to parallel the phases of the classic hero’s journey.

The study’s version of the hero’s journey involved several basic elements, including a shift that drives protagonists to set an important goal; the onset of challenges as they pursue that goal; personal growth or transformation along the journey; enlisting allies along the way; and a triumphant return with some insight or contribution that serves the community.

After people completed this exercise—which you can try for yourself on Rogers’ website—they reported that they found their lives more meaningful than they had beforehand. Control participants, who simply wrote about different aspects of their lives, did not report this change. That suggested that the re-storying exercise was indeed responsible for the meaning boost.

Rogers’s most striking finding, though, wasn’t just that the exercise helped people find meaning. It was that this deeper meaning influenced the everyday choices people made in challenging moments.

At one point, Rogers asked people in his re-storying trial how they planned to handle a major problem in their lives. Those who had completed the re-storying process were more likely to say they would look for direct ways to address the issue—say, by speaking to a supervisor to resolve a conflict, rather than remaining passive. They also looked at the problem itself more positively, seeing it as a chance to learn and correct course.

article continues after advertisement

The clarifying function of the re-storying process seems to bolster focus and resolve in the face of challenge. These traits are integral to a well-paced life, helping you channel your energy more directly toward pursuits that will strengthen and fulfill you. And when you want to restore the focus re-storying supplies, you can revisit or repeat the process, integrating fresh insights into your guiding narrative.

This is an adapted excerpt from my new Simon & Schuster book The Art of Pacing.
